Base directory for this skill: /home/javad/energy-run/community/.claude/skills/energy-efficiency

# Energy Efficiency Analysis

You are finding **energy waste**: code that spends energy on work the program
does not need, and that a specific refactoring can remove without changing what
the program does.

**The task is to cover everything you were asked to look at** — every file,
every function and every method — and to report every case you find there, not
a few that turn up early in one or two files. A run that stops after two or
three findings has not done it. Keep going until every file has been read, and
report what you find whether or not it can be measured here.

Why this matters more than speed: waste in code you never read is never
found. Nothing later in the procedure goes back to code left out of step 1, and
the report then reads as if that code were clean, so a missed inefficiency
costs more than any minutes spent reading. Keep working until all of it is
done — every file read, every suspicion decided, every accepted one given an
outcome. Do not stop partway to report progress or to ask whether to go on;
stop to ask only when you cannot continue without an answer.

Paths below are relative to this file's directory — call it `$SKILL`. Work out
what `$SKILL` is once, at the start, and use it throughout.

**Time:** you have 120 minutes for the whole run, thinking and measuring
included, and the session is stopped at 120. That is enough to be thorough, so
do not rush: give each unit the reading it needs. Run `date` when you start
and again as you go, so you know how much of the 120 minutes is left.

---

## What counts as a finding

> A finding is a **repair**: a concrete edit to *this* code, with a stated
> reason why the edit saves energy. That it does is a separate claim, and only
> a measurement makes it.

Three consequences you have to hold onto:

- **No repair, no finding.** If you cannot write the actual edit for this code,
  you have not found anything — you have recognised a pattern.
- **No measurement, no claim.** A repair is said to save energy only once it
  has been measured. One left unmeasured is still a finding — with no claim
  attached to it.
- **Report the failures too.** A repair you built, measured, and found saves
  nothing is a result. It stays in `submissions.jsonl`, with its verdict.

## One repair, one reason

Attribute each repair to a single reason: the thing about the code that
explains why the edit saves energy.

One unit can have several repairs, and they can overlap: fixing how a function
searches can make a redundant conversion and a needless copy disappear too,
because they only existed to serve the search. The rule is the same either
way — **every accepted suspicion gets its own repair, written against the
original code, and its own measurement.** That is what says what each one is
worth on its own.

- Two suspicions that would get **exactly the same edit** are one repair:
  submit it once, and record the other as `same_repair_as`.
- Two that get **different edits to the same code** are two repairs: submit
  both.
- Do **not** widen a repair to cover a second suspicion, and do not split one
  edit into several submissions to raise the count.

Since each repair is written against the original, at most one per function
can ever be applied. Choosing it is not part of your job: submit every repair,
measured, and the measurements decide.

## How much you may change

The edit should be as small as removing the waste allows. That bounds its
**size**, never its location, and never how much code you may read to decide.

**What must survive is the unit's contract**: the same return value, the same
effect on its arguments and on the module- and class-level values it uses, the
same printed and logged output, the same files, the same exception type. That
is what gets checked, for every repair, and it is the whole of what callers are
entitled to.

Anything **only the unit depends on** is implementation detail: a helper
nothing else calls, state nothing else reads. You may change a helper's
signature, its return shape or its behaviour, if that is what removes the
waste. A list built in `__init__` and searched only in this method is one
repair, made in both. A value shaped wrongly by a producer and compensated for
by its consumers is one repair, made in all of them — when nothing but the unit
reaches them.

Two obligations come with reaching outside the unit:

- **Give every function you change its own entry** in the submission, named
  `path::qualname`, in whichever file it lives.
- **Establish that nothing else depends on what you changed** — no other
  caller of a changed function, no other reader of changed state — and say how
  in `sole_caller_evidence`. Anything else that depends on it is not
  implementation detail: the change reaches it too, and the check on this unit
  would not notice.

What you may not do is bring anything else along. A patch that also renames
variables, tidies an unrelated branch, or fixes a second problem cannot be
attributed to one reason, and the measurement stops meaning anything. The
second problem is a second finding, or it is nothing.

## What is not energy waste

**Style.** Unreadable, undocumented, poorly named, badly typed code is not
energy waste. If the repair does not change what the machine does, it
is out of scope here.

Everything else that wastes work is in scope, wherever it is in the program:
a real repair is a real repair, and the measurement will say what it came to.

## Energy is not time

They usually move together, but not always. Spreading work across cores cuts
wall-clock time while raising energy. A busy-wait poll burns power while making
no progress. A blocked event loop keeps a core hot for nothing. Judge energy,
and when the two diverge, say so — those cases are the most interesting ones
you can find.

## Measuring for yourself

At any step, whenever you are unsure — whether some code costs anything,
whether a change would save energy or only time, whether a version still does
the same work — measure it. `$SKILL/scripts/energy.py` takes one energy reading
of any Python call:

```python
import sys; sys.path.insert(0, "...")    # $SKILL/scripts, written out in full
from energy import measure
r = measure(my_function, data)          # r.joules, r.seconds, r.watts, r.result
```

What you run, on what data, how many times and how you compare is up to you;
the script's docstring says what one reading holds. These readings are for
your own judgement, and nothing records them: a repair is still measured by
`verify.py`, in step 3, on the inputs generated for it.

---

## Procedure

Four steps, in order. **Each step writes its own file in the repository's
root, and when the step is finished you say so** — then the next step begins:

| Step | Writes | When it is finished |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Find | `step1.jsonl` | `python $SKILL/scripts/step.py done 1` |
| 2. Decide | `step2.jsonl` | `python $SKILL/scripts/step.py done 2` |
| 3. Repair and measure | `submissions.jsonl`, `step3.jsonl` | `python $SKILL/scripts/step.py done 3` |
| 4. Finish | your final message | — |

Step 1 is breadth: every file read, and every unit where something may be
wasteful put on a list. Steps 2 and 3 are depth, for the units on that list.

While a step is open, its file is yours: write it, rewrite it, fix it. `done`
keeps the file, outside this session, as that step's output, and makes it
read-only — a finished step is never changed. If a later step shows you
something an earlier one missed, say so in the later step's file: step 2
rejects a step-1 suspicion and adds a new one; it does not touch
`step1.jsonl`. Do not start a step's file before the previous step is done.
`inputs.py` and
`verify.py` run between `done 2` and `done 3`.

Every step after the first is a check on what the first wrote down, and a
check you run against nothing checks nothing.

Each record is one JSON line with **exactly the keys its example below shows —
all of them, and no others**; a key with nothing to say is `null` or `[]`.
`$SKILL/reference/output-format.md` lists every key and what it holds. Every
file goes in the repository's root, the directory you were started in —
nowhere else.

### 1. Find — *in:* a target · *out:* every unit where something may be wasteful, with its suspicions

**The target** is what you were asked to look at: the whole repository, a
directory, a file, or a single unit. Choose units only from inside it; read
outside it as far as you need. A unit named loosely — "the render function" —
is yours to pin down: find it, and record the exact `path::qualname` it
resolved to. If more than one function matches, all of them are the target.

Read the repository first — its entry points, what its tests exercise, what
its README says it is for — so that you know what each part of it is for.

**Know what you are looking for:** work the program does not need, work done
more often than necessary, or work done in a more expensive way than its result
requires. Ask of every function whether any of these is happening there.

**Then you must go through every file in the target, and every unit in each
file.** List the target's Python files first, so you know what there is to
read, and work through that list file by file, reading every function and
method in each. Do not stop at the first files that turn something up: the
target is not done until every file in it has been read.

**The list you finish step 1 with is final.** No later step can add a unit to
it, so a file not read here is a file no one examines.

**You may hand the reading to subagents** — on a large target it is the
quickest way to read all of it. If you can start subagents (in Claude Code, the
Agent tool; its read-only `Explore` type fits), split the file list into groups
and start one subagent per group, all in the same turn so they read in
parallel. Tell each to read every function and method in its files in full,
looking for these three kinds of waste, and to report for each its `path::qualname`, its
lines, and what looks wasteful in it. Their reports are leads, not findings:
look at the code of every lead before you list it, and only you write the step
files and run the scripts.

**Leave nothing out because of what you expect later.** Code that calls a
network or a service, code you doubt any input could be generated for, a
script, a long file: read it all the same, and list what looks wasteful in
it. Whether a repair can be measured is step 3's question — ask for its inputs
and let the generator say — and one that cannot is still a finding, recorded
as `blocked` with the message that showed it.

**Record every unit where something may be wasteful**, and in it every
suspicion: the lines, and why. A suspicion is a reason to look closer, not a
verdict — step 2 decides — so write it down whenever you have the reason, and
do not hold one back because you are unsure. Nothing limits how many units or
suspicions you record — one, ten, a hundred or a thousand, whatever the code
holds. A unit where nothing looks wasteful gets no record.

If you were asked for a number of units, list at most that many. You may
change which units those are until you finish step 1; just do not go over the
number.

```jsonc
{"step": 1, "unit": "src/render.py::Report.render", "suspicions": [
  {"label": "a", "lines": [47],
   "why": "`self.buf` is grown with += once per row; nothing reads it in the loop"},
  {"label": "b", "lines": [44,45],
   "why": "`sorted(self.columns)` is recomputed per row and does not depend on the row"}
]}
```

Give each suspicion a `label` — `a`, `b`, `c` — unique within the unit. Steps 2
and 3 refer to it by that label.

Write one record per unit to `step1.jsonl`, and rewrite it as often as you like
while step 1 is open. Before you finish, check the file list: every file on it
has been read, by you or by a subagent. If one has not, step 1 is not finished.
Then run `python $SKILL/scripts/step.py done 1`.

### 2. Decide — *in:* each unit on the list, with its suspicions · *out:* one record per unit, each suspicion accepted or rejected

Start this step after `step.py done 1`, and write one step-2 record to
`step2.jsonl` for every unit on your list. When every record is written, run
`python $SKILL/scripts/step.py done 2`; step 3 starts after it.

**First, read the unit properly.** Read the whole unit, then follow it
outward in both directions:

- **Down, into what it calls.** If the unit calls something you have not read,
  read it. A three-line loop body calling `normalise(row)` may be compiling a
  regex and rebuilding two dicts per iteration, and none of that is visible
  from the loop. Keep going until you reach the standard library or code that
  plainly does no work.
- **Up, into what calls it.** See what it is given and what is done with what
  it returns: waste can sit between a unit and its callers — a result the
  caller throws away, a shape the caller has to undo.

Then say in one sentence what it computes and where its work goes: that is
`what_it_does`.

Read outward because the expensive waste is not in any one line. Some waste
is — a conversion, a lookup, a concatenation — and you can see it where it
sits. The larger kind is in the *arrangement*: a value computed in one place
and thrown away in another; a shape chosen early that every later step has to
compensate for; six functions doing what a different split does in two; a
result recomputed on each of three paths that each look reasonable alone. No
single statement shows any of it.

Read the unit a second time, now with the repair in mind. What the edit would
have to be is usually what tells you whether your first reading was right.

Every suspicion ends this step **accepted** or **rejected**, and nothing is
edited in place. If the second reading changes your mind, reject the suspicion
and add a new one, with a new label, saying what you now think. That keeps what
you first thought on the record, which is the part worth reading later.

A unit's suspicions may also **grow** here: reading a second time to write a
repair is one of the better ways to notice something you missed. Its units do
not — they were settled in step 1. A rejection with a reason is as much a
result as an acceptance.

**For each suspicion:**

1. **Does it apply here?** Does your account of the waste still hold on a second
   reading, or was it the shape of the code rather than what it does?
1. **Can you write the repair for *this* code**, as an edit rather than a
   rewrite of the unit? No repair, no finding.
1. **Does the repair preserve behaviour** on every input, including the edge
   cases and whatever the callers rely on?
1. **State the mechanism** — what work stops happening, and why that costs
   less. "Built-ins are faster" is not a mechanism, and it is wrong often
   enough to matter.

Accept if all of them hold, and give the mechanism as `why`. Otherwise reject,
and give the check that decided it as `why`.

```jsonc
{"step": 2, "unit": "src/router.py::Router.allowed",
 "what_it_does": "checks each request against `self.blocked`, a list built once in __init__",
 "decisions": [
  {
    "label": "a", "lines": [58], "verdict": "rejected",
    "why": "the repair belongs where the container is built, not where it is searched. Added `b` instead."
  },
  {
    "label": "b", "lines": [31], "verdict": "accepted",
    "why": "`self.blocked` is a list searched once per request, built in __init__ at line 31 and read nowhere else; as a set each search is one hash lookup"
  }
]}
```

Every suspicion from step 1 gets a decision under its label, and a unit whose
suspicions are all rejected still gets its record — a run that examined three
functions and one that examined three hundred have to be distinguishable.

### 3. Repair and measure — *in:* every accepted suspicion · *out:* `submissions.jsonl`, measured, and one record per unit

Start this step once every unit has been through step 2, and work from their
step-2 records.

**You do not edit the repository.** You describe each repair; the script
applies it to a copy and reads `before` from the repository as it stands. That
is what makes the baseline something you could not have shaped to suit the
result. Work in a scratch copy of your own if it helps you think, but the
repository you were pointed at stays untouched — and you measure against it,
`--repo .`, never against a copy: a number taken on edited code is discarded.

Read `$SKILL/reference/verifying.md` before your first submission.

1. **Choose what to measure.** Measuring takes under a minute a repair, so at
   most **20** repairs are measured — the ones you expect to save the most
   energy, across all units. Twenty is a limit, not a target: if fewer
   suspicions were accepted, measure those. A place is used only by a repair
   that gets a verdict (`confirmed`, `partial`, `mixed`, `regressed`,
   `negligible`), and it keeps the place even if its line is later deleted or
   edited: once 20 repairs have one, verify.py measures no more. A repair whose
   unit gets no inputs, or that cannot be made to behave identically, uses no
   place, so take the next accepted suspicion instead. Every other accepted
   suspicion is still a finding: record it as `deferred` in step 3's record.

2. **Ask for the inputs of every unit you will measure** — all of them in one
   request. Inputs are asked for here, in step 3: `inputs.py` opens at
   `step.py done 2`.

   ```bash
   python $SKILL/scripts/inputs.py request src/render.py::Report.render src/parse.py::tokenize
   ```

   You do not write the inputs a repair is measured on. A generator outside
   this session writes them for each unit: **four** measured inputs that make
   the unit do substantial and different work, and a few edge inputs checked
   only for identical behaviour. It keeps an input only if it runs on the
   original code and gives the same output twice. The request returns at once,
   and generation takes a minute or two, all units together — up to five for a
   hard unit. Each unit's file appears in `.energy-inputs/`, read-only: read it
   to see what your repairs will face. You cannot change the inputs; after the
   session, every repair is measured again on our own copy of them.

   `python $SKILL/scripts/inputs.py status` shows which units are ready, and
   for each one that `failed`, why and what to do next. A repair is measured
   by running the original and the repair on the same inputs, here, and
   comparing their output and their energy, so an input counts only if the
   original completes on it from this machine alone and gives the same output
   every time. A unit that needs the network, a remote service, credentials,
   hardware or data the repository does not hold cannot do that, and its
   repairs cannot be measured here. That says nothing against the suspicion:
   it is still a finding, recorded as `blocked` with the reason. When the
   reason is a package missing from this venv, install it and ask for the unit
   again; when the generator simply did not manage, it may on another try
   (three in all). A unit that failed gives its place back: up to 30 units can
   have inputs or be generating at once, failed ones not counted, so ask for
   the next unit you would measure in its place. Up to 30 different units may
   fail in a session.

3. **For each chosen suspicion, write the smallest repair of the original
   code** that removes its waste, as one line in `submissions.jsonl`. Every
   repair is written against the code as it is now, never on top of another —
   so the order does not matter, and nothing you submit changes what the next
   one is written against.
   - **The same edit as one you already wrote** for this unit: do not submit it
     again. Record its outcome in step 3 as `same_repair_as`, with that
     submission's `id` as `submission`.
   - **A different edit to the same code**: submit it as a repair of its own.

4. **Measure the whole file, once.**

   ```bash
   python $SKILL/scripts/verify.py submissions.jsonl --repo .
   ```

   It first waits — up to ten minutes, saying for what — for any inputs still
   being generated, then measures every line in turn, under a minute each, on
   its unit's inputs, and writes the result into that line as soon as it is
   measured, as `agent_measurement`: the verdict in `agent_measurement.status`,
   and the joules and seconds of every input. Never write or edit it yourself.
   Give the command a timeout to match, or run it in the background — and if it
   is still running, wait for it before you finish.

5. **Then fix only what is broken, and run the same command again.** It
   measures only the lines that need it.

   | Result | What you do |
   |---|---|
   | `not_equivalent` | the repair changes behaviour: fix that line |
   | `invalid` | the line is malformed, or the inputs do not load against your repair: fix it as the message says |
   | `no_inputs` | the unit has none: request them if you have not, otherwise record `blocked` with the message |
   | `error` | the environment could not run it: do what the message says — install a missing package here and run again, or record `blocked` |
   | `inconclusive` | the host was too noisy; the next run measures it again |
   | `over_limit` | 20 repairs already have a verdict, so it was not measured: record its suspicion as `deferred` |
   | `confirmed` `partial` `mixed` `regressed` `negligible` | **final.** Do not touch the line |

   A measured result is never revised. Editing a measured line to get a better
   number makes it `invalid`, and the result it had stays on record. If you
   think a genuinely different repair would do better, that is a new line —
   both are kept. A suspicion is `blocked` only when the
   tools showed it cannot be measured: its unit's inputs could not be generated,
   its module does not load, or its repair cannot be made to behave identically
   — quote that message as `why`. One you did not try, because you expect it
   cannot run or it is outside the 20, is `deferred`: ask for its inputs instead
   whenever you can.

6. **Record what happened to every accepted suspicion** in `step3.jsonl`, one
   record per unit:

   ```jsonc
   {"step": 3, "unit": "src/render.py::Report.render", "outcomes": [
     {"label": "a", "outcome": "submitted",      "submission": "render-concat", "why": null},
     {"label": "b", "outcome": "same_repair_as", "submission": "render-concat", "why": null},
     {"label": "c", "outcome": "blocked",        "submission": null, "why": "inputs.py: no inputs could be generated: every call opens a database connection"},
     {"label": "d", "outcome": "deferred",       "submission": null, "why": "outside the 20 repairs measured"}
   ]}
   ```

Every measured repair stays in `submissions.jsonl`, whatever its verdict —
one you delete is still measured after the session. `partial`, `negligible`,
`regressed` and `mixed` are results, and a file that kept only the wins could
not be told apart from one that hid its losses.

7. **Check, then finish the step.** Every suspicion accepted in step 2 has an
   outcome in `step3.jsonl`, and every line of `submissions.jsonl` carries the
   `agent_measurement` the script wrote, with nothing left `inconclusive` or
   `error` that a run could still settle. Then run
   `python $SKILL/scripts/step.py done 3`.

### 4. Finish — *in:* the three steps' files · *out:* a short summary

This step writes no file. End with a short summary for whoever asked: for each submission, the unit,
what it repairs, the verdict, and what it saved across its four inputs. Lead
with what was confirmed, say plainly what was not, and say how many accepted
suspicions were deferred unmeasured.

`$SKILL/reference/output-format.md` has the exact shape of every file.

---

## How this goes wrong

Failure modes, in the order they actually happen:

1. **Stopping early.** Reading a few files, picking two or three units from
   them and taking those through to the end. It feels like progress and leaves
   most of the target unread, and the list cannot grow after step 1. Read every
   file first, yourself or through subagents, and pick from all of them.
1. **Repeating what you have read about Python performance.** Much of it is
   out of date, and some of it was never true. Every claim here gets measured,
   and the ones you are most certain about are the ones worth measuring first.
1. **Submitting one edit twice.** One edit is one repair, attributed to
   one reason; another suspicion it also fixes is `same_repair_as`.
1. **Building one repair on top of another.** Every repair is written against
   the original code. One written against your previous repair is measured
   against code that does not exist.
1. **Ignoring context.** Almost every pattern that looks wasteful is the right
   call somewhere. A bare `except` in a retry loop, a materialised list that
   gets indexed twice, a wrapper that is public API.
   Ask what the author was required to do before deciding they were wrong.
1. **Skipping measurement because the waste is obvious.** The obvious ones are
   exactly where a wrong assumption hides.
1. **Rewriting the unit.** A patch that changes everything cannot be attributed
   to one reason, and cannot be measured against one. Change what removes
   the waste and stop.
1. **Changing more than the unit without checking what else depends on it.**
   The check watches the unit's contract, so another caller or another reader
   of the changed state breaks silently.

## Scope

Python. A finding is a repair with a reason, not a label.

A **unit** is a function or a method. That is the granularity at which units are
examined, cleared and reported, and at which a repair is measured — the cases
call something, and this is the something. A function defined inside another
function is not one: nothing can call it on its own, so the function around it
is the unit.

That is all it bounds. Read as far as you need in either direction, and
repair across as many units as the waste requires. When the waste exists
only in the arrangement — two methods of a class that each look
reasonable and are wrong together, a helper whose shape forces the code around
it to compensate — report it against the unit whose behaviour the repair must
preserve, and give every function you change its own entry in the submission.

# Output format

A run leaves four files in the repository's root — the directory you were
started in, next to its README — and nowhere else: not in a subdirectory, not
in a scratch directory. They are your record of the work, not edits to the
code, so writing them there does not touch the repository:

- **`step1.jsonl`**, **`step2.jsonl`**, **`step3.jsonl`** — what each step
  produced, one JSON line per record. Each is finished with
  `python $SKILL/scripts/step.py done N`, and read-only after that.
- **`submissions.jsonl`** — the repairs, one per line, written in step 3. The
  script measures each and writes the result into it.

Nothing else is written. Your summary at the end of the run is your final
message, not a file.

---

## step1.jsonl to step3.jsonl

One JSON object per line, in the file of the step that produced it, each
tagged with its step.

**Every record has exactly the keys listed for it — all of them, every time,
and no others.** A key with nothing to say is `null` or `[]`, never left out.
The same keys in every run are what make runs comparable.

| Record | One per | Keys |
|---|---|---|
| step 1, in `step1.jsonl` | unit where something may be wasteful | `step`, `unit`, `suspicions` |
| step 2, in `step2.jsonl` | unit on the step-1 list | `step`, `unit`, `what_it_does`, `decisions` |
| step 3, in `step3.jsonl` | unit with an accepted suspicion | `step`, `unit`, `outcomes` |
| a suspicion, in `suspicions` | | `label`, `lines`, `why` |
| a decision, in `decisions` | | `label`, `lines`, `verdict`, `why` |
| an outcome, in `outcomes` | | `label`, `outcome`, `submission`, `why` |

Step 4 writes no record: its output is your final message.

Shown expanded here; each is written on a single line.

```jsonc
{"step": 1, "unit": "src/render.py::Report.render", "suspicions": [
  {"label": "a", "lines": [47],
   "why": "`self.buf` is grown with += once per row; nothing reads it in the loop"},
  {"label": "b", "lines": [44,45],
   "why": "`sorted(self.columns)` is recomputed per row and does not depend on the row"}
]}
```

```jsonc
{"step": 2, "unit": "src/router.py::Router.allowed",
 "what_it_does": "checks each request against `self.blocked`, a list built once in __init__",
 "decisions": [
  {
    "label": "a", "lines": [58], "verdict": "rejected",
    "why": "the repair belongs where the container is built, not where it is searched. Added `b` instead."
  },
  {
    "label": "b", "lines": [31], "verdict": "accepted",
    "why": "`self.blocked` is a list searched once per request, built in __init__ at line 31 and read nowhere else; as a set each search is one hash lookup"
  }
]}
```

```jsonc
{"step": 3, "unit": "src/render.py::Report.render", "outcomes": [
  {"label": "a", "outcome": "submitted",      "submission": "render-concat", "why": null},
  {"label": "b", "outcome": "same_repair_as", "submission": "render-concat", "why": null},
  {"label": "c", "outcome": "blocked",        "submission": null, "why": "inputs.py: no inputs could be generated: every call opens a database connection"},
  {"label": "d", "outcome": "deferred",       "submission": null, "why": "outside the 20 repairs measured"}
]}
```

### Field rules

**`label`** names a suspicion within its unit — `a`, `b`, `c` — and is how steps
2 and 3 refer to it. A suspicion added in step 2 gets a label of its own.

**`lines`** is a list of line numbers in the unit's file.

**`why`** is the reason, under one name everywhere. On a suspicion: what looks
wasteful. On a decision: what decided it — for `accepted`, the mechanism, what
work stops happening; for `rejected`, the check that failed. On an outcome: why
it was `blocked` or `deferred`, and `null` otherwise. It must be specific to
this code: name the variable, the line, the structure. "Inefficient string
handling" is not a reason; "`self.buf` is grown with `+=` across `rows`" is.

**`verdict`** is `"accepted"` or `"rejected"`.

**`what_it_does`**, in step 2, is one sentence: what the unit computes, and
where its work goes. It is written after reading the unit in full, which is
what it shows.

**`outcome`**, in step 3, is one of: `submitted` (`submission` is its `id` in
`submissions.jsonl`), `same_repair_as` (`submission` is the `id` of the
submission that already makes this edit), `blocked` (the tools showed no repair
can be measured here — inputs that could not be generated, a module that does
not load, a repair that cannot be made to behave identically — and `why`
quotes that message) or `deferred` (accepted, and not measured: outside the 20,
or never tried). A suspicion you did not ask inputs for is `deferred`, not
`blocked`. A deferred suspicion is still a finding.

Every unit from step 1 has a step-2 record, and every suspicion is accounted
for: rejected in step 2, or given an outcome in step 3. A run that examined
three functions and one that examined three hundred have to be
distinguishable, and so do a suspicion you dropped and one you forgot.

---

## submissions.jsonl

Every line has every field listed in `$SKILL/reference/verifying.md` — none
are optional, and no others are accepted. Three rules connect it to the
step files:

- every outcome `submitted` in `step3.jsonl` names a line here, and every line
  here is named by exactly one;
- every line ends with the `agent_measurement` the script wrote. Never write
  or edit it, and never write a verdict anywhere yourself;
- every measured repair stays, whatever its verdict.

What the script writes into a line:

```jsonc
"agent_measurement": {
  "status": "confirmed",
  "reason": "25.9% +-3.0% energy saved on 'many-rows', clearing the 1.4% noise floor. ...",
  "profile": "fast",
  "noise_floor_pct": 1.4,
  "noise_floor_from": "session calibration",
  "equivalence_relaxed": [],      // what this environment weakened (stand-in packages, skipped statements); repeat wherever the saving is quoted
  "stubbed": [],                  // uninstalled packages stood in for while loading; normally empty
  "per_case": [
    {"label": "typical", "repeats": 9500, "clamped": false,
     "before_energy_j": 51.03, "after_energy_j": 47.29,
     "before_time_s": 1.04, "after_time_s": 0.96,
     "energy_ci_pct": 1.2, "significant": true}
    // ... one row per input, all four
  ],
  "submission_hash": "3f2a9c01d4e5b6a7"
  // abridged: a few more fields record provenance -- the meter, its coverage, the canary case
}
```

`per_case` carries joules and seconds for each version on every case, and no
percentage: the joules are the result, and a percentage stored beside them is a
second copy that can disagree. `energy_ci_pct` is not a saving — it is the
half-width of the 95% interval on the paired comparison, which `significant`
is judged from.
# Verifying a saving

A repair comes with a claim: that this refactoring saves energy. This is how
the claim gets tested. Read this before writing your first submission.

The rule: **no repair is reported as saving anything until it has been
measured on this machine.**

You do not edit the repository. You describe the repair; the script applies it
to a copy, and `before` is whatever the repository already contains.

---

## The submission

One JSON object per line of `submissions.jsonl`, one line per repair:

```jsonc
{
  "id": "render-concat",
  "unit": "src/render.py::Report.render",
  "changed": {
    "src/render.py::Report.render": "def render(self):\n    return \"\".join(_row(r) for r in self.rows)"
  },
  "sole_caller_evidence": null,
  "notes": "Sizes taken from the fixtures in tests/; `_row` left as the real helper."
}
```

**Every line has every field below, and no others** — none is optional; the
ones with nothing to say take the empty value shown.

| Field | What it holds |
|---|---|
| `id` | a name for this repair, unique in the file |
| `unit` | the function or method whose behaviour must be preserved, as `path::qualname` |
| `changed` | `path::qualname` → the full replacement source of that function |
| `sole_caller_evidence` | how you know nothing else calls or reads what you changed; `null` when `changed` holds only the unit |
| `notes` | a few sentences a reader would otherwise have to guess; `""` if none |
| `agent_measurement` | written by the script, never by you |

`changed` holds **source text, not a diff and not an AST**: the whole function
as you would commit it, decorators and `def` line included, written at column
zero even when it is a method. Each entry replaces exactly that function and
nothing around it — so a repair that needs a module the file does not import
yet imports it inside the function. After the first call, an `import`
statement is a single dictionary lookup.

## You do not supply `before`

`before` is the function already in the repository, loaded from the file you
named. You cannot simplify it or substitute an illustration of the pattern,
because you never write it. A repair worth 30% of a five-line sketch and 2% of
the real function always measures against the real function.

The rest is real too: the helpers are the real helpers, the constants the real
constants, the imports the real imports. So the replacement must differ from
the repository by **the repair alone**. If it also renames a variable, inlines
a helper or fixes a second thing, the measurement no longer attributes to
one reason and the result is unusable.

## Changing more than the unit

The unit's **contract** is what has to survive: everything a caller can see,
listed under "What "the same" means" below.
Anything only the unit depends on — a helper nothing else calls, state nothing
else reads — is implementation detail, and may change.

Give each changed function its own entry in `changed`, in whatever file it
lives, and fill in `sole_caller_evidence`: the search you ran, or the call sites
and attribute reads you checked. The check watches the unit's contract only, so
anything else broken by the change would pass every check here. A submission
that changes more than the unit without this is rejected.

## Several repairs in one unit

Each repair is written against the original code and measured against it, on
its own. There is no order to take them in, and no repair is built on another.

- **The same edit** for two suspicions is one repair. Submit it once; the other
  suspicion is `same_repair_as` it.
- **Different edits to the same code** are separate repairs. Submit each.
- **Every repair of one unit is measured on that unit's inputs**, so their
  savings are measured on identical inputs and can be compared.

## The inputs

You do not write them. Ask for every unit you will measure, in one request:

```bash
python $SKILL/scripts/inputs.py request src/render.py::Report.render src/parse.py::tokenize
python $SKILL/scripts/inputs.py status          # which are ready
```

A generator outside this session writes each unit's inputs from the
repository's own code — the unit, its class, what it uses, and where the
repository calls it. It asks for more candidates than it needs, runs each on
the original code, keeps those that complete and give the same output on a
second, fresh run, and of those keeps the four that do the most work. They are
fixed for the unit: every repair of it is measured on the same four, and so is
the re-measurement after the session, which uses our own copy of them.

Requests open in step 3, at `step.py done 2`. The request returns at once.
Generation runs outside this session, every unit at the same time, and usually
takes a minute or two; a hard unit can take five. Ask for all of them in one
request; a unit you add later is another request. Up to 30 units can have
inputs or be generating at once: more than the 20 repairs measured, so there is
room for units you decide against. A unit that fails gives its place back, so
ask for another in its place; up to 30 different units may fail in a session.

verify.py does not measure while anything is still being generated: it waits
first, up to ten minutes, printing which units it is waiting for. Give its
first run a timeout to match — fifteen minutes plus a minute per repair — or
run it in the background. A unit still not ready after that comes back
`no_inputs` and is measured by the next run.

**A module that does work when it is imported can still be measured** — a
script that reads `sys.argv`, opens files or calls a server at its top level.
When importing it fails, it is loaded one top-level statement at a time: the
statements that fail are skipped and reported, and the unit is measured if it
is still defined. So ask for its inputs rather than assuming it cannot run; the
generator says so when it cannot.

**A unit listed as `failed` can be asked for again** once you have fixed what
stopped it. If the reason is a package missing from this environment, install
it into this venv — whatever you install stays for the re-measurement after
the session — and request the unit again; it is generated once more, up to
three times a session. When the generator simply did not manage — none of its
inputs ran on the original, or it produced none — another try may succeed: it
writes new inputs every time. `inputs.py status` says which case each failure
is.

Each unit's inputs are one file in `.energy-inputs/`, read-only. Read it before
you write the repair: it is exactly what the repair will be measured on. They
cannot be changed, and editing the file would change nothing that counts —
the result after the session is measured on our copy.
The file defines two functions, each returning `(label, thunk)` pairs:

- **`checks()`** — edge inputs: empty, one element, `None`, an odd type. Both
  versions run them and must behave the same; they are never measured.
- **`cases()`** — the four measured inputs, each making the unit do different
  work. Every one counts on its own: a repair is `confirmed` only if it saves
  energy on all four, and one that measurably loses on any of them is `mixed`.

A thunk returns the unit's arguments as a tuple, or `call(...)` when the unit
takes keyword arguments. **A method takes its instance as the first
argument**, so the thunk builds the instance and passes it.

**Why each input is called many times.** One call is usually too short for the
energy meter to see, so each input is called many times in a row and the
energy of all the calls is added up. That is the only reason for the
repetition. Every call gets a fresh copy of the input, built before the
calls are measured, and the outputs are compared once, before anything is
measured.

**A coroutine is run, a generator is drained.** An `async def` unit is run to
completion on an event loop of its own, and a generator's output is collected
and compared as what it yielded — so a repair that turns a list into a
generator counts as returning something different.

**Files are output like any other.** Inputs put the files a unit reads under
`WORKDIR`, a directory the script gives each side, and every file the unit
creates, changes or deletes, under `WORKDIR` or inside the repository, has to
come out the same on both sides.

**A unit with no inputs.** An input counts only if the original completes on
it here, from this machine alone, and gives the same output on every run: that
is what lets the two versions be compared. A unit that needs the network, a
remote service, credentials, hardware or data the repository does not hold, or
whose own output changes from run to run, cannot give that, whatever the input.
`inputs.py status` lists it as `failed`, with the reason and what to do next,
and verify.py reports its repairs as `no_inputs` with the same. Record their
suspicions as `blocked`, quoting the reason — the suspicion is still a
finding; only its saving cannot be measured here — and ask for the next unit
you would measure in its place: a failed unit does not count toward the 30.

**`blocked` needs that evidence.** A suspicion is `blocked` only when the tools
showed it cannot be measured here: its inputs could not be generated, its
module does not load, the result is `error` for something you cannot install,
or the repair cannot be made to behave identically. Quote the message as
`why`. One you did not ask inputs for — because you expect it cannot run, or
because it is outside the 20 — is `deferred`, not blocked: ask for its inputs
instead whenever you can, and let the generator say whether it runs.

## What "the same" means

The replacement must do everything the original does, on every input:

- the same **return value**;
- the same effect on its **arguments**, an object's own attributes included;
- the same changes to the **module-level and class-level values** the
  original's code uses;
- the same **files** written;
- the same **printed output** and the same **log records**;
- the same **exception** type.

Nothing in a submission relaxes this. A repair that stops changing the
caller's data — `lst.sort()` becomes `sorted(lst)` — stops updating a
module-level cache, or drops a log call changes what callers can see, and
comes back `not_equivalent`; so does one that returns the same answer in a
different form. Two things are left out on purpose: the numbers inside a log
message, so a logged duration is not behaviour, and a new module-level value
the repair keeps for itself, such as a cache only it reads.

## Running it

```bash
python $SKILL/scripts/verify.py --calibrate                    # optional, see below
python $SKILL/scripts/verify.py submissions.jsonl --repo .     # the whole file
```

`--calibrate` measures two copies of identical code against each other, the
way repairs are measured. The answer must come back
*insignificant*; its width is this host's resolution limit, and the bar every
real effect has to clear. It is kept for the session, and taken automatically
if you forget. If it comes back significant, something else is using the
machine, and nothing measured until it stops means anything.

The second command goes through the file once — about a minute per repair,
plus half a minute to calibrate, after any inputs still being generated are
ready — so give the command a timeout to match, or run it in the background
and wait for it. It writes each result into its line,
as `agent_measurement`, with the verdict in `agent_measurement.status`. Run it again after fixing broken lines and it
measures only what needs it: a line never measured, a line that was
`not_equivalent`, `invalid` or `error` and has since been fixed, and anything
`inconclusive` or `error`, which is simply tried again.

A line with a measured result — `confirmed`, `partial`, `mixed`,
`regressed`, `negligible` — is final and is never measured again. If it has been edited
since, the script reports it `invalid` and leaves the result it had exactly as
it was. A different repair is a new line.

## When the environment gets in the way

- **A package is missing** — the result is `error`, naming it: install it into
  this environment, `python -m pip install <package>`, and run again. Never
  install the repository's own code, and never create another environment.
- **Anything else cannot run here** — the result says what failed: record the
  suspicion as `blocked`, with the message.

Always measure with `--repo .`, against the repository itself: a result taken
against an edited copy is discarded.

## What the script does

1. **Stages** two fresh copies of the repository, the second with your
   replacements spliced in, and loads both side by side in one process.
2. **Equivalence.** Every input from `checks()` and `cases()` runs once
   through both versions, and everything in "What "the same" means" above is
   compared. A mismatch is `not_equivalent`, and nothing is measured.
3. **Measurement.** The two versions take turns, one window of about a second
   each, three pairs per input, the order flipped every pair, so the machine's
   own drift affects both alike.
4. **Statistics.** The energy difference is averaged over the pairs, with a 95%
   confidence interval. Energy decides the verdict; time is reported beside it
   and decides nothing.

## Verdicts

| Verdict | What it means | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| `confirmed` | saves energy on all four inputs, each clearing the noise floor | nothing — final |
| `partial` | saves energy on some inputs, and moves nothing beyond the noise on the others | nothing — final. A narrower claim: it pays on some of the work the unit does |
| `mixed` | saves energy on some inputs, costs it on others — both clearing the floor | nothing — final. A trade-off: which side wins depends on the input |
| `regressed` | every case that moved measurably, got worse | nothing — final |
| `negligible` | measured on a clean floor, and nothing moved more than the noise | nothing — final |
| `inconclusive` | the host's noise was too high to resolve an effect this size | nothing; the next run measures it again. It is **not** `negligible` |
| `not_equivalent` | the replacement behaves differently from the original | fix the repair and run again |
| `invalid` | the line is malformed, the inputs do not load against the repair, or a measured line was edited | fix it as the message says |
| `no_inputs` | the unit has no inputs: none were requested, or none could be generated | request them; if they could not be generated, record `blocked` with the message |
| `error` | the environment failed: an import, the meter, a library the unit needs | what the message says: install a missing package and run again, or record `blocked` |
| `over_limit` | 20 repairs in this session already have a verdict, the most it measures; this one was not measured | record its suspicion as `deferred` |

Every verdict stays. A file that proposes ten repairs and has three come back
`negligible` says more than one that quietly dropped them.

`negligible` and `inconclusive` are different claims. `negligible` says the
repair does nothing, on a machine quiet enough to tell — that is evidence.
`inconclusive` says this machine could not tell, which is a fact about the host
and says nothing about the code. Reporting the second as the first writes a
busy host down as evidence against the repair.

`mixed` is not a softer `regressed`. Both effects are real: the repair pays on
one input and costs on another, and which one the code actually sees decides
whether it is worth having.

## What the numbers mean

The meter reads the whole machine's CPU package energy over each window, idle
cores included. A version that finishes sooner also spends less idle power, so
the comparison holds, but it cannot tell a change in power from a change in
duration. When energy improves while wall-clock time does not, say so — that is
more interesting than a performance bug.

## When received wisdom is wrong

It happens, and measurement is how you find out.

Every style guide says growing a string with `+=` in a loop is quadratic, so
collect the parts and join them. Measured, the textbook example got *slower* —
62 ms against 56 ms at 400 000 iterations. CPython resizes a string in place
when nothing else refers to it, so the classic example was already linear. The
real waste turned out to be about aliasing: through an attribute, where the
optimisation cannot fire, the same repair saves 94.8% ± 0.1%.

If a repair you were confident about comes back `negligible`, that is a result.
Report it, and say what you measured. Do not quietly drop it and try a
different one until something sticks.

it was `blocked` or `deferred`, and `null` otherwise. It must be specific to
this code: name the variable, the line, the structure. "Inefficient string
handling" is not a reason; "`self.buf` is grown with `+=` across `rows`" is.

**`verdict`** is `"accepted"` or `"rejected"`.

**`what_it_does`**, in step 2, is one sentence: what the unit computes, and
where its work goes. It is written after reading the unit in full, which is
what it shows.

**`outcome`**, in step 3, is one of: `submitted` (`submission` is its `id` in
`submissions.jsonl`), `same_repair_as` (`submission` is the `id` of the
submission that already makes this edit), `blocked` (the tools showed no repair
can be measured here — inputs that could not be generated, a module that does
not load, a repair that cannot be made to behave identically — and `why`
quotes that message) or `deferred` (accepted, and not measured: outside the 20,
or never tried). A suspicion you did not ask inputs for is `deferred`, not
`blocked`. A deferred suspicion is still a finding.

Every unit from step 1 has a step-2 record, and every suspicion is accounted
for: rejected in step 2, or given an outcome in step 3. A run that examined
three functions and one that examined three hundred have to be
distinguishable, and so do a suspicion you dropped and one you forgot.

---

## submissions.jsonl

Every line has every field listed in `$SKILL/reference/verifying.md` — none
are optional, and no others are accepted. Three rules connect it to the
step files:

- every outcome `submitted` in `step3.jsonl` names a line here, and every line
  here is named by exactly one;
- every line ends with the `agent_measurement` the script wrote. Never write
  or edit it, and never write a verdict anywhere yourself;
- every measured repair stays, whatever its verdict.

What the script writes into a line:

```jsonc
"agent_measurement": {
  "status": "confirmed",
  "reason": "25.9% +-3.0% energy saved on 'many-rows', clearing the 1.4% noise floor. ...",
  "profile": "fast",
  "noise_floor_pct": 1.4,
  "noise_floor_from": "session calibration",
  "equivalence_relaxed": [],      // what this environment weakened (stand-in packages, skipped statements); repeat wherever the saving is quoted
  "stubbed": [],                  // uninstalled packages stood in for while loading; normally empty
  "per_case": [
    {"label": "typical", "repeats": 9500, "clamped": false,
     "before_energy_j": 51.03, "after_energy_j": 47.29,
     "before_time_s": 1.04, "after_time_s": 0.96,
     "energy_ci_pct": 1.2, "significant": true}
    // ... one row per input, all four
  ],
  "submission_hash": "3f2a9c01d4e5b6a7"
  // abridged: a few more fields record provenance -- the meter, its coverage, the canary case
}
```

`per_case` carries joules and seconds for each version on every case, and no
percentage: the joules are the result, and a percentage stored beside them is a
second copy that can disagree. `energy_ci_pct` is not a saving — it is the
half-width of the 95% interval on the paired comparison, which `significant`
is judged from.
# Verifying a saving

A repair comes with a claim: that this refactoring saves energy. This is how
the claim gets tested. Read this before writing your first submission.

The rule: **no repair is reported as saving anything until it has been
measured on this machine.**

You do not edit the repository. You describe the repair; the script applies it
to a copy, and `before` is whatever the repository already contains.

---

## The submission

One JSON object per line of `submissions.jsonl`, one line per repair:

```jsonc
{
  "id": "render-concat",
  "unit": "src/render.py::Report.render",
  "changed": {
    "src/render.py::Report.render": "def render(self):\n    return \"\".join(_row(r) for r in self.rows)"
  },
  "sole_caller_evidence": null,
  "notes": "Sizes taken from the fixtures in tests/; `_row` left as the real helper."
}
```

**Every line has every field below, and no others** — none is optional; the
ones with nothing to say take the empty value shown.

| Field | What it holds |
|---|---|
| `id` | a name for this repair, unique in the file |
| `unit` | the function or method whose behaviour must be preserved, as `path::qualname` |
| `changed` | `path::qualname` → the full replacement source of that function |
| `sole_caller_evidence` | how you know nothing else calls or reads what you changed; `null` when `changed` holds only the unit |
| `notes` | a few sentences a reader would otherwise have to guess; `""` if none |
| `agent_measurement` | written by the script, never by you |

`changed` holds **source text, not a diff and not an AST**: the whole function
as you would commit it, decorators and `def` line included, written at column
zero even when it is a method. Each entry replaces exactly that function and
nothing around it — so a repair that needs a module the file does not import
yet imports it inside the function. After the first call, an `import`
statement is a single dictionary lookup.

## You do not supply `before`

`before` is the function already in the repository, loaded from the file you
named. You cannot simplify it or substitute an illustration of the pattern,
because you never write it. A repair worth 30% of a five-line sketch and 2% of
the real function always measures against the real function.

The rest is real too: the helpers are the real helpers, the constants the real
constants, the imports the real imports. So the replacement must differ from
the repository by **the repair alone**. If it also renames a variable, inlines
a helper or fixes a second thing, the measurement no longer attributes to
one reason and the result is unusable.

## Changing more than the unit

The unit's **contract** is what has to survive: everything a caller can see,
listed under "What "the same" means" below.
Anything only the unit depends on — a helper nothing else calls, state nothing
else reads — is implementation detail, and may change.

Give each changed function its own entry in `changed`, in whatever file it
lives, and fill in `sole_caller_evidence`: the search you ran, or the call sites
and attribute reads you checked. The check watches the unit's contract only, so
anything else broken by the change would pass every check here. A submission
that changes more than the unit without this is rejected.

## Several repairs in one unit

Each repair is written against the original code and measured against it, on
its own. There is no order to take them in, and no repair is built on another.

- **The same edit** for two suspicions is one repair. Submit it once; the other
  suspicion is `same_repair_as` it.
- **Different edits to the same code** are separate repairs. Submit each.
- **Every repair of one unit is measured on that unit's inputs**, so their
  savings are measured on identical inputs and can be compared.

## The inputs

You do not write them. Ask for every unit you will measure, in one request:

```bash
python $SKILL/scripts/inputs.py request src/render.py::Report.render src/parse.py::tokenize
python $SKILL/scripts/inputs.py status          # which are ready
```

A generator outside this session writes each unit's inputs from the
repository's own code — the unit, its class, what it uses, and where the
repository calls it. It asks for more candidates than it needs, runs each on
the original code, keeps those that complete and give the same output on a
second, fresh run, and of those keeps the four that do the most work. They are
fixed for the unit: every repair of it is measured on the same four, and so is
the re-measurement after the session, which uses our own copy of them.

Requests open in step 3, at `step.py done 2`. The request returns at once.
Generation runs outside this session, every unit at the same time, and usually
takes a minute or two; a hard unit can take five. Ask for all of them in one
request; a unit you add later is another request. Up to 30 units can have
inputs or be generating at once: more than the 20 repairs measured, so there is
room for units you decide against. A unit that fails gives its place back, so
ask for another in its place; up to 30 different units may fail in a session.

verify.py does not measure while anything is still being generated: it waits
first, up to ten minutes, printing which units it is waiting for. Give its
first run a timeout to match — fifteen minutes plus a minute per repair — or
run it in the background. A unit still not ready after that comes back
`no_inputs` and is measured by the next run.

**A module that does work when it is imported can still be measured** — a
script that reads `sys.argv`, opens files or calls a server at its top level.
When importing it fails, it is loaded one top-level statement at a time: the
statements that fail are skipped and reported, and the unit is measured if it
is still defined. So ask for its inputs rather than assuming it cannot run; the
generator says so when it cannot.

**A unit listed as `failed` can be asked for again** once you have fixed what
stopped it. If the reason is a package missing from this environment, install
it into this venv — whatever you install stays for the re-measurement after
the session — and request the unit again; it is generated once more, up to
three times a session. When the generator simply did not manage — none of its
inputs ran on the original, or it produced none — another try may succeed: it
writes new inputs every time. `inputs.py status` says which case each failure
is.

Each unit's inputs are one file in `.energy-inputs/`, read-only. Read it before
you write the repair: it is exactly what the repair will be measured on. They
cannot be changed, and editing the file would change nothing that counts —
the result after the session is measured on our copy.
The file defines two functions, each returning `(label, thunk)` pairs:

- **`checks()`** — edge inputs: empty, one element, `None`, an odd type. Both
  versions run them and must behave the same; they are never measured.
- **`cases()`** — the four measured inputs, each making the unit do different
  work. Every one counts on its own: a repair is `confirmed` only if it saves
  energy on all four, and one that measurably loses on any of them is `mixed`.

A thunk returns the unit's arguments as a tuple, or `call(...)` when the unit
takes keyword arguments. **A method takes its instance as the first
argument**, so the thunk builds the instance and passes it.

**Why each input is called many times.** One call is usually too short for the
energy meter to see, so each input is called many times in a row and the
energy of all the calls is added up. That is the only reason for the
repetition. Every call gets a fresh copy of the input, built before the
calls are measured, and the outputs are compared once, before anything is
measured.

**A coroutine is run, a generator is drained.** An `async def` unit is run to
completion on an event loop of its own, and a generator's output is collected
and compared as what it yielded — so a repair that turns a list into a
generator counts as returning something different.

**Files are output like any other.** Inputs put the files a unit reads under
`WORKDIR`, a directory the script gives each side, and every file the unit
creates, changes or deletes, under `WORKDIR` or inside the repository, has to
come out the same on both sides.

**A unit with no inputs.** An input counts only if the original completes on
it here, from this machine alone, and gives the same output on every run: that
is what lets the two versions be compared. A unit that needs the network, a
remote service, credentials, hardware or data the repository does not hold, or
whose own output changes from run to run, cannot give that, whatever the input.
`inputs.py status` lists it as `failed`, with the reason and what to do next,
and verify.py reports its repairs as `no_inputs` with the same. Record their
suspicions as `blocked`, quoting the reason — the suspicion is still a
finding; only its saving cannot be measured here — and ask for the next unit
you would measure in its place: a failed unit does not count toward the 30.

**`blocked` needs that evidence.** A suspicion is `blocked` only when the tools
showed it cannot be measured here: its inputs could not be generated, its
module does not load, the result is `error` for something you cannot install,
or the repair cannot be made to behave identically. Quote the message as
`why`. One you did not ask inputs for — because you expect it cannot run, or
because it is outside the 20 — is `deferred`, not blocked: ask for its inputs
instead whenever you can, and let the generator say whether it runs.

## What "the same" means

The replacement must do everything the original does, on every input:

- the same **return value**;
- the same effect on its **arguments**, an object's own attributes included;
- the same changes to the **module-level and class-level values** the
  original's code uses;
- the same **files** written;
- the same **printed output** and the same **log records**;
- the same **exception** type.

Nothing in a submission relaxes this. A repair that stops changing the
caller's data — `lst.sort()` becomes `sorted(lst)` — stops updating a
module-level cache, or drops a log call changes what callers can see, and
comes back `not_equivalent`; so does one that returns the same answer in a
different form. Two things are left out on purpose: the numbers inside a log
message, so a logged duration is not behaviour, and a new module-level value
the repair keeps for itself, such as a cache only it reads.

## Running it

```bash
python $SKILL/scripts/verify.py --calibrate                    # optional, see below
python $SKILL/scripts/verify.py submissions.jsonl --repo .     # the whole file
```

`--calibrate` measures two copies of identical code against each other, the
way repairs are measured. The answer must come back
*insignificant*; its width is this host's resolution limit, and the bar every
real effect has to clear. It is kept for the session, and taken automatically
if you forget. If it comes back significant, something else is using the
machine, and nothing measured until it stops means anything.

The second command goes through the file once — about a minute per repair,
plus half a minute to calibrate, after any inputs still being generated are
ready — so give the command a timeout to match, or run it in the background
and wait for it. It writes each result into its line,
as `agent_measurement`, with the verdict in `agent_measurement.status`. Run it again after fixing broken lines and it
measures only what needs it: a line never measured, a line that was
`not_equivalent`, `invalid` or `error` and has since been fixed, and anything
`inconclusive` or `error`, which is simply tried again.

A line with a measured result — `confirmed`, `partial`, `mixed`,
`regressed`, `negligible` — is final and is never measured again. If it has been edited
since, the script reports it `invalid` and leaves the result it had exactly as
it was. A different repair is a new line.

## When the environment gets in the way

- **A package is missing** — the result is `error`, naming it: install it into
  this environment, `python -m pip install <package>`, and run again. Never
  install the repository's own code, and never create another environment.
- **Anything else cannot run here** — the result says what failed: record the
  suspicion as `blocked`, with the message.

Always measure with `--repo .`, against the repository itself: a result taken
against an edited copy is discarded.

## What the script does

1. **Stages** two fresh copies of the repository, the second with your
   replacements spliced in, and loads both side by side in one process.
2. **Equivalence.** Every input from `checks()` and `cases()` runs once
   through both versions, and everything in "What "the same" means" above is
   compared. A mismatch is `not_equivalent`, and nothing is measured.
3. **Measurement.** The two versions take turns, one window of about a second
   each, three pairs per input, the order flipped every pair, so the machine's
   own drift affects both alike.
4. **Statistics.** The energy difference is averaged over the pairs, with a 95%
   confidence interval. Energy decides the verdict; time is reported beside it
   and decides nothing.

## Verdicts

| Verdict | What it means | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| `confirmed` | saves energy on all four inputs, each clearing the noise floor | nothing — final |
| `partial` | saves energy on some inputs, and moves nothing beyond the noise on the others | nothing — final. A narrower claim: it pays on some of the work the unit does |
| `mixed` | saves energy on some inputs, costs it on others — both clearing the floor | nothing — final. A trade-off: which side wins depends on the input |
| `regressed` | every case that moved measurably, got worse | nothing — final |
| `negligible` | measured on a clean floor, and nothing moved more than the noise | nothing — final |
| `inconclusive` | the host's noise was too high to resolve an effect this size | nothing; the next run measures it again. It is **not** `negligible` |
| `not_equivalent` | the replacement behaves differently from the original | fix the repair and run again |
| `invalid` | the line is malformed, the inputs do not load against the repair, or a measured line was edited | fix it as the message says |
| `no_inputs` | the unit has no inputs: none were requested, or none could be generated | request them; if they could not be generated, record `blocked` with the message |
| `error` | the environment failed: an import, the meter, a library the unit needs | what the message says: install a missing package and run again, or record `blocked` |
| `over_limit` | 20 repairs in this session already have a verdict, the most it measures; this one was not measured | record its suspicion as `deferred` |

Every verdict stays. A file that proposes ten repairs and has three come back
`negligible` says more than one that quietly dropped them.

`negligible` and `inconclusive` are different claims. `negligible` says the
repair does nothing, on a machine quiet enough to tell — that is evidence.
`inconclusive` says this machine could not tell, which is a fact about the host
and says nothing about the code. Reporting the second as the first writes a
busy host down as evidence against the repair.

`mixed` is not a softer `regressed`. Both effects are real: the repair pays on
one input and costs on another, and which one the code actually sees decides
whether it is worth having.

## What the numbers mean

The meter reads the whole machine's CPU package energy over each window, idle
cores included. A version that finishes sooner also spends less idle power, so
the comparison holds, but it cannot tell a change in power from a change in
duration. When energy improves while wall-clock time does not, say so — that is
more interesting than a performance bug.

## When received wisdom is wrong

It happens, and measurement is how you find out.

Every style guide says growing a string with `+=` in a loop is quadratic, so
collect the parts and join them. Measured, the textbook example got *slower* —
62 ms against 56 ms at 400 000 iterations. CPython resizes a string in place
when nothing else refers to it, so the classic example was already linear. The
real waste turned out to be about aliasing: through an attribute, where the
optimisation cannot fire, the same repair saves 94.8% ± 0.1%.

If a repair you were confident about comes back `negligible`, that is a result.
Report it, and say what you measured. Do not quietly drop it and try a
different one until something sticks.

    61	def fmt_dur(seconds: float) -> str:
    62	    h = int(seconds // 3600)
    63	    m = int((seconds % 3600) // 60)
    64	    s = int(seconds % 60)
    65	    if h:
    66	        return f"{h}h {m}m"
    67	    if m:
    68	        return f"{m}m {s}s"

    72	def collect_jobs(since: datetime) -> list[dict]:
    73	    """Return per-job records for every bare-metal job since `since`."""
    74	    since_q = since.strftime("%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ")
    75	    records: list[dict] = []
    76	    for repo, wf_file in WORKFLOWS:
    77	        print(f"  - {repo} :: {wf_file}", file=sys.stderr)
    78	        runs_path = (
    79	            f"/repos/{repo}/actions/workflows/{wf_file}/runs"
    80	            f"?per_page=100&status=completed&created=%3E%3D{since_q}"
    81	        )
    82	        try:
    83	            runs = list(gh_paginated(runs_path, "workflow_runs"))
    84	        except RuntimeError as e:
    85	            print(f"    ! {e}", file=sys.stderr)
    86	            continue
    87	        for run in runs:
    88	            run_id = run["id"]
    89	            wf_name = run.get("name") or wf_file
    90	            run_started_at = run.get("run_started_at") or run.get("created_at")
    91	            try:
    92	                jobs = list(gh_paginated(
    93	                    f"/repos/{repo}/actions/runs/{run_id}/jobs?per_page=100",
    94	                    "jobs",
    95	                ))
    96	            except RuntimeError as e:
    97	                print(f"    ! run {run_id}: {e}", file=sys.stderr)
    98	                continue
    99	            for job in jobs:
   100	                labels = job.get("labels") or []
   101	                if not any(
   102	                    isinstance(lbl, str) and lbl.startswith(BAREMETAL_LABEL_PREFIX)
   103	                    for lbl in labels
   104	                ):
   105	                    continue
   106	                if job.get("conclusion") in ("skipped", "neutral"):
   107	                    continue
   108	                if not (job.get("runner_name") and job.get("runner_group_id")):
   109	                    continue
   110	                started, completed = job.get("started_at"), job.get("completed_at")
   111	                if not started or not completed:
   112	                    continue
   113	                try:
   114	                    dur = (parse_iso(completed) - parse_iso(started)).total_seconds()
   115	                except ValueError:
   116	                    continue
   117	                if dur <= 0:
   118	                    continue
   119	                qwait = 0.0
   120	                if run_started_at:
   121	                    try:
   122	                        qwait = max(
   123	                            0.0,
   124	                            (parse_iso(started) - parse_iso(run_started_at))
   125	                            .total_seconds(),
   126	                        )
   127	                    except ValueError:
   128	                        qwait = 0.0
   129	                records.append({
   130	                    "repo": repo,
   131	                    "wf_file": wf_file,
   132	                    "wf_name": wf_name,
   133	                    "run_id": run_id,
   134	                    "started": parse_iso(started),
   135	                    "duration": dur,
   136	                    "qwait": qwait,
   137	                })
   138	    return records

   141	def render_table(records: list[dict], since: datetime) -> str:
   142	    agg: dict[tuple[str, str, str], dict] = defaultdict(
   143	        lambda: {"runs": set(), "total": 0.0,
   144	                 "qwait_max": 0.0,
   145	                 "run_totals": defaultdict(float)}
   146	    )
   147	    for r in records:
   148	        if r["started"] < since:
   149	            continue
   150	        key = (r["repo"], r["wf_file"], r["wf_name"])
   151	        a = agg[key]
   152	        a["runs"].add(r["run_id"])
   153	        a["total"] += r["duration"]
   154	        a["run_totals"][r["run_id"]] += r["duration"]
   155	        if r["qwait"] > a["qwait_max"]:
   156	            a["qwait_max"] = r["qwait"]
   157	
   158	    rows = sorted(agg.items(), key=lambda kv: -kv[1]["total"])
   159	    out: list[str] = []
   160	    out.append(
   161	        "| Repository | Workflow | Runs | Total | Avg/run | "
   162	        "Max run | Max queue wait |"
   163	    )
   164	    out.append("|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|")
   165	    for (repo, wf_file, wf_name), v in rows:
   166	        n_runs = len(v["runs"])
   167	        avg = v["total"] / n_runs if n_runs else 0
   168	        max_run = max(v["run_totals"].values(), default=0.0)
   169	        repo_short = repo.split("/", 1)[1] if "/" in repo else repo
   170	        wf_link = (
   171	            f"https://github.com/{repo}/blob/main/.github/workflows/{wf_file}"
   172	        )
   173	        out.append(
   174	            f"| {repo_short} | [`{wf_file}`]({wf_link}) | "
   175	            f"{n_runs} | {fmt_dur(v['total'])} | {fmt_dur(avg)} | "
   176	            f"{fmt_dur(max_run)} | {fmt_dur(v['qwait_max'])} |"
   177	        )
   178	    return "\n".join(out)
   179

   181	def main() -> int:
   182	    p = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
   183	    p.add_argument(
   184	        "--windows", type=int, nargs="+", default=[7, 30],
   185	        help="One or more day windows to emit tables for.",
   186	    )
   187	    p.add_argument("--output", default="baremetal-runner-report.md")
   188	    args = p.parse_args()
   189	
   190	    now = datetime.now(timezone.utc)
   191	    max_days = max(args.windows)
   192	    since_max = now - timedelta(days=max_days)
   193	
   194	    print(f"Fetching jobs since {since_max.isoformat()} "
   195	          f"(max window {max_days} days)", file=sys.stderr)
   196	    records = collect_jobs(since_max)
   197	    print(f"Collected {len(records)} bare-metal job records", file=sys.stderr)
   198	
   199	    sections: list[str] = []
   200	    for days in sorted(args.windows):
   201	        since = now - timedelta(days=days)
   202	        sections.append(f"## Last {days} days")
   203	        sections.append("")
   204	        sections.append(render_table(records, since))

   207	    text = "\n".join(sections).rstrip() + "\n"
   208	    with open(args.output, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
   209	        f.write(text)
   210	    print(f"Wrote {args.output}", file=sys.stderr)
   211	    return 0

   243	"""Tag eligible voters on a GitHub issue for the OpenTelemetry GC election.
   244	
   245	Behaviour:
   246	- If the issue has no existing voter-notification comments, post one comment
   247	  per batch of 50 voters from the roll file.
   248	- If the issue already has voter-notification comments, reconcile with the
   249	  current roll file:
   250	    * Remove `@handle` lines from existing comments for handles no longer in
   251	      the roll. If a comment loses all its voters, delete it.
   252	    * Post additional comments (batched by 50) for handles in the roll that
   253	      are not yet mentioned in any existing voter-notification comment.
   254	
   255	Voter-notification comments are identified by an exact match on the header
   256	string, so unrelated conversation comments are left untouched.
   257	"""
   258	
   259	import argparse
   260	import csv
   261	import json
   262	import os
   263	import re
   264	import subprocess
   265	import sys
   266	
   267	VOTERS_ROLL_PATH = os.environ.get('VOTERS_ROLL_PATH', './voters-roll.csv')
   268	BATCH_SIZE = 50
   269	HEADER = (
   270	    "We invite the people mentioned in this comment to vote in the "
   271	    "OpenTelemetry Governance Committee, as they have provided more than 20 "
   272	    "contributions to the project over the last year via GitHub. Your "
   273	    "contributions were comments, code reviews, pull requests, among others. "
   274	    "Thank you!"
   275	)
   276	
   277	MENTION_RE = re.compile(r'^\* @([A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9-]*)\s*$', re.MULTILINE)
   278	ISSUE_URL_RE = re.compile(r'^https?://github\.com/([^/]+)/([^/]+)/issues/(\d+)/?$')
   279	TRUE_VALS = {'true', '1', 'yes', 'y'}
   280	FALSE_VALS = {'false', '0', 'no', 'n'}
   281	
   282	
   283	def parse_bool(v):
   284	    s = str(v).strip().lower()
   285	    if s in TRUE_VALS:
   286	        return True
   287	    if s in FALSE_VALS:
   288	        return False
   289	    sys.exit(
   290	        f"invalid boolean value: {v!r} "
   291	        f"(expected one of {sorted(TRUE_VALS | FALSE_VALS)})"
   292	    )
   293	
   294	
   295	def parse_issue_url(url):
   296	    m = ISSUE_URL_RE.match(url.strip())
   297	    if not m:
   298	        sys.exit(f"invalid issue URL: {url}")
   299	    return m.group(1), m.group(2), m.group(3)
